Eighteen more joined on 2026-10-20 (bank version 4, DECISIONS DH13), and he checked them that night (the hub QA list for the card daily-huddle-new-data-sets-lab-normals-d, all Good with no notes); `abim` on each is the ABIM January 2026 sheet's value, a cross-check for his read that the bank does not carry.

questions.q: What is the normal arterial blood pH for an adult?
questions.sub: Typical adult range. Labs vary a little.
questions.src: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf), Arterial Blood Gas Analysis: Fundamentals, Interpretation, and Clinical Utility
questions.quote: although values may vary slightly among laboratories and across age groups, from neonates to older adults: pH (7.35-7.45)
questions.why: StatPearls notes that the ranges shift slightly between laboratories and across age groups.

questions.q: What is the normal arterial PaCO2 for an adult?
questions.sub: Typical adult range. Labs vary a little.
questions.src: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf), Arterial Blood Gas Analysis: Fundamentals, Interpretation, and Clinical Utility
questions.quote: PaCO2 (35-45 mm Hg)
questions.why: PaCO2 tracks ventilation, so hypoventilation pushes it up and hyperventilation brings it down.

questions.q: What is the normal arterial PaO2 for an adult?
questions.sub: Adult breathing room air. Labs vary a little.
questions.src: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf), Arterial Blood Gas Analysis: Fundamentals, Interpretation, and Clinical Utility
questions.quote: PaO2 (75-100 mm Hg)
questions.why: PaO2 tracks oxygenation, which pulse oximetry can estimate without a needle, though the arterial blood gas is still the gold standard.

questions.q: What is the normal arterial bicarbonate (HCO3) for an adult?
questions.sub: Typical adult range. Labs vary a little.
questions.src: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf), Arterial Blood Gas Analysis: Fundamentals, Interpretation, and Clinical Utility
questions.quote: HCO3 (22-26 mEq/L)
questions.why: Most blood gas analyzers calculate HCO3 from the measured pH and PaCO2, so it often differs from a chemistry panel's total CO2 by about 1.2 mmol/L.

questions.q: What is a normal SpO2 for a healthy adult?
questions.sub: Measured by pulse oximetry.
questions.quote: A normal SpO2 in healthy adults is 95% to 100%.
questions.why: Pulse oximeters may overestimate saturation in people with darker skin, especially at lower saturations.

questions.q: What is the normal respiratory rate for an adult, in breaths per minute?
questions.sub: Typical adult range at rest.
questions.quote: The respiratory rate is the number of breaths/min, with a normal adult range of 12 to 20.
questions.why: Above 20 breaths a minute is tachypnea, and respiratory rate is one of the vital signs most often skipped or measured wrong.

questions.q: What is the normal resting heart rate for an adult, in beats per minute?
questions.sub: Typical adult range at rest.
questions.quote: The normal adult resting heart rate is 60 to 100 bpm
questions.why: A resting rate above 100 is tachycardia and a rate below 60 is bradycardia.

questions.q: What does the CDC count as normal blood pressure for an adult?
questions.quote: Normal blood pressure is less than 120/80 mm Hg.
questions.why: The CDC calls blood pressure that stays at or above 130/80 mm Hg high blood pressure.

questions.q: What fasting blood sugar does the CDC call normal for an adult?
questions.sub: Measured after an overnight fast.
questions.quote: This measures your blood sugar after an overnight fast (not eating). Normal: 99 mg/dL or below
questions.why: On the same test, 100 to 125 mg/dL means prediabetes and 126 mg/dL or above means diabetes.

questions.q: What is the normal serum sodium for an adult?
questions.sub: Typical adult range. Labs vary a little.
questions.quote: Serum Sodium Normal range: 135 to 145 mmol/L
questions.why: Hyponatremia, a sodium under 135 mmol/L, is the most frequent electrolyte disorder.

questions.q: What is the normal serum potassium for an adult?
questions.sub: Typical adult range. Labs vary a little.
questions.src: Clinical Methods, 3rd edition (NCBI Bookshelf), Serum Potassium
questions.quote: Normal serum potassium is 3.5 to 5.5 mEq/L; however, plasma potassium is 0.5 mEq/L lower.
questions.why: Plasma potassium reads about 0.5 mEq/L lower than serum, and StatPearls puts the lower limit at 3.6 mmol/L, so sources differ a little.

questions.q: What is the normal serum chloride for an adult?
questions.sub: Typical adult range. Labs vary a little.
questions.src: Clinical Methods, 3rd edition (NCBI Bookshelf), Serum Chloride
questions.quote: Normal serum chloride concentrations range from 96 to 106 mEq/L.
questions.why: Chloride is the main anion that travels with sodium in the fluid outside the cells.

questions.q: What is the normal blood urea nitrogen (BUN) for an adult?
questions.sub: Typical adult range. Labs vary a little.
questions.src: Clinical Methods, 3rd edition (NCBI Bookshelf), BUN and Creatinine
questions.quote: The normal range of urea nitrogen in blood or serum is 5 to 20 mg/dl, or 1.8 to 7.1 mmol urea per liter.
questions.why: The range is wide because protein intake, hydration, liver urea production and kidney excretion all move it.

questions.q: What is the normal hemoglobin range for adult women?
questions.sub: Typical adult range. It shifts with altitude.
questions.quote: Hemoglobin (varies with altitude) Adult men: 14 to 17 gm/dL Adult women: 12 to 15 gm/dL
questions.why: The NHLBI range for adult men is 14 to 17 g/dL, and age, altitude and race can all shift normal ranges.

questions.q: What is the normal white blood cell count for an adult?
questions.sub: Typical adult range. Labs vary a little.
questions.quote: Adults: 4500 to 11,000 cells/μL
questions.why: Newborns run far higher, at 13,000 to 38,000 cells per microliter.

questions.q: What is the normal platelet count for an adult?
questions.sub: Typical adult range. Labs vary a little.
questions.quote: A normal platelet count in adults ranges from 150,000 to 450,000 platelets per microliter of blood.
questions.why: A count under 150,000 is lower than normal, the condition called thrombocytopenia.

questions.q: HIPAA, the law behind federal standards that protect sensitive health information, dates from what year?
questions.src: CDC Public Health Law, Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA)
questions.quote: The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) of 1996 establishes federal standards protecting sensitive health information from disclosure without patient's consent.
questions.why: HHS issued the HIPAA Privacy Rule to put the law's requirements into practice.

questions.q: In what year did Congress enact EMTALA, the law that guarantees emergency screening regardless of ability to pay?
questions.src: CMS, Emergency Medical Treatment & Labor Act (EMTALA)
questions.quote: In 1986, Congress enacted the Emergency Medical Treatment & Labor Act (EMTALA) to ensure public access to emergency services regardless of ability to pay.
questions.why: It obliges hospitals that take Medicare and offer emergency services to give a medical screening exam and, for an emergency condition, stabilizing treatment.

questions.q: In what year did President Lyndon B. Johnson sign the law that created Medicare and Medicaid?
questions.quote: On July 30, 1965, President Lyndon B. Johnson signed into law legislation that established the Medicare and Medicaid programs.
questions.why: Original Medicare had Part A for hospital insurance and Part B for medical insurance, and in 1972 it was expanded to cover people with disabilities and end-stage renal disease.

questions.q: In what year was the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) created?
questions.quote: The Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) was created in 1997 to give health insurance and preventive care to nearly 11 million
questions.why: It was built for uninsured children in working families that earned too much to qualify for Medicaid, and every state now has a CHIP plan.

questions.q: The Health Insurance Marketplace, where people apply for and enroll in private health plans, came from which law?
questions.quote: The 2010 Affordable Care Act (ACA) brought the Health Insurance Marketplace
questions.why: The Affordable Care Act became law in 2010 and also gave CMS new ways to design and test how care is paid for and delivered.

questions.q: The HITECH Act, which pushed hospitals and doctors toward electronic health records, was passed as part of which larger law?
opts: The American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009
questions.src: HHS, HITECH Act Enforcement Interim Final Rule
questions.quote: (HITECH) Act, enacted as part of the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009, was signed into law on February 17, 2009
questions.why: It was signed on February 17, 2009, to promote the adoption and meaningful use of health information technology.

questions.q: In what year did the 21st Century Cures Act make sharing electronic health information the expected norm in health care?
questions.quote: In 2016, the 21st Century Cures Act (Cures Act) made sharing electronic health information the expected norm in health care
questions.why: It also told HHS to name the reasonable and necessary activities that do not count as information blocking, now listed in 45 CFR Part 171.

questions.q: The No Surprises Act, which protects patients from most surprise out-of-network bills, went into effect in what year?
questions.quote: The No Surprises Act is a federal law that went into effect on January 1, 2022.
questions.why: It applies to most types of health insurance and covers emergency room visits and some care tied to a visit at an in-network hospital.

questions.q: Under the Hill-Burton law of 1946, hospitals got federal grants and loans to build and modernize. What did they agree to in return?
opts: Provide a reasonable volume of care to people unable to pay
questions.src: HRSA, Hill-Burton Free and Reduced-Cost Health Care
questions.quote: In return, they agreed to provide a reasonable volume of services to people unable to pay
questions.why: The program stopped providing funds in 1997, but about 127 facilities nationwide are still obligated to provide free or reduced-cost care.

questions.q: Medicare Part D, the prescription drug benefit, went into effect in what year?
questions.quote: The MMA also expanded Medicare to include an optional prescription drug benefit, “Part D,” which went into effect in 2006.
questions.why: It came from the Medicare Prescription Drug Improvement and Modernization Act of 2003, under which Medicare-approved private plans became known as Medicare Advantage.

questions.q: What does FHIR stand for?
questions.quote: Welcome to the FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) Specification, which is a standard for exchanging healthcare information electronically.
questions.why: It is a standard for exchanging healthcare information electronically, and the current published version is R5.

questions.q: Which organization publishes FHIR, the standard for health care data exchange?
opts: The Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT
questions.quote: FHIR is a standard for health care data exchange, published by HL7®.
questions.why: HL7 releases the FHIR specification under an open CC0 license.

questions.q: RxNorm gives normalized names to what?
questions.src: National Library of Medicine, RxNorm Overview
questions.quote: RxNorm is two things: a normalized naming system for generic and branded drugs
questions.why: The National Library of Medicine produces RxNorm, and it leaves out medical devices, dietary supplements and homeopathic products.

questions.q: Which organization produces LOINC, the code set used for lab test orders and results?
questions.src: National Library of Medicine, UMLS: LOINC
questions.quote: LOINC® (Logical Observations Identifiers, Names, Codes), is a clinical terminology important for laboratory test orders and results, produced by the Regenstrief Institute.
questions.why: NLM supports LOINC's development by contract, and HL7 named it a preferred code set for lab test names in 1999.

questions.q: On what date did U.S. health care switch from ICD-9 to ICD-10 codes?
questions.quote: On October 1, 2015, the health care industry transitioned from ICD-9 to ICD-10 codes for diagnoses and inpatient procedures.
questions.why: ICD-10 applies to everyone covered by HIPAA, not just providers who bill Medicare or Medicaid.

questions.q: How many digits are in a National Provider Identifier (NPI)?
questions.quote: The NPI is a 10-position, intelligence-free numeric identifier (10-digit number).
questions.why: The digits carry no information about the provider, such as the state they live in or their medical specialty.

questions.q: How was the Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT (ONC) first created in 2004?
opts: By an executive order from President George W. Bush
questions.quote: The Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT was created by Executive Order 13335, signed by President George W. Bush in April 2004.
questions.why: ONC was set up inside HHS, and in 2024 it published the HTI-1 rule carrying out parts of the 21st Century Cures Act.

questions.q: As of 2024, what share of U.S. non-federal acute care hospitals had adopted a certified EHR?
questions.src: ONC Health IT Quick-Stat #61, National Trends in Hospital and Physician Adoption of Electronic Health Records (updated June 2026)
questions.quote: As of 2024, 91% of office-based physicians and nearly all non-federal acute care hospitals (>99%) adopted a certified EHR.
questions.why: In 2008 the same measure stood at 9% of hospitals, and office-based physicians reached 91% by 2024.

questions.q: Under federal rules, information blocking is a practice that is likely to do what?
opts: Filter spam email before it reaches clinical staff
Delay an insurer's payment of a claim
Interfere with the access, exchange or use of electronic health information
Hide a hospital's prices from the public
questions.quote: Information blocking is a practice by an “actor” that is likely to interfere with the access, exchange, or use of electronic health information (EHI)
questions.why: The 21st Century Cures Act defines it, and it holds health care providers to a different knowledge standard than health IT developers.

questions.q: What is the DICOM standard used for?
opts: Medical images such as CT, MRI and ultrasound
questions.src: DICOM Standard (NEMA, DICOM Secretariat), About DICOM: Overview
questions.quote: is the international standard for medical images and related information. It defines the formats for medical images that can be exchanged
questions.why: It was first published in 1993 and is recognized by the International Organization for Standardization as ISO 12052.

questions.q: What does ICD-10-CM code W61.62XA describe?
questions.src: NLM Clinical Tables, ICD-10-CM API (chapter and block from the CDC NCHS ICD-10-CM browser, FY2027)
questions.quote: Struck by duck, initial encounter
questions.why: It sits under W61, contact with birds, in Chapter 20, External causes of morbidity (V00 to Y99), and the final A marks the initial encounter.

questions.q: What does ICD-10-CM code W56.22XA describe?
questions.src: NLM Clinical Tables, ICD-10-CM API (chapter and block from the CDC NCHS ICD-10-CM browser, FY2027)
questions.quote: Struck by orca, initial encounter
questions.why: It sits under W56, contact with nonvenomous marine animal, in Chapter 20, and the final A marks the initial encounter.

questions.q: What does ICD-10-CM code V91.07XA describe?
opts: Fall from water-skis into a boat wake
Burn due to water-skis on fire
questions.src: NLM Clinical Tables, ICD-10-CM API (chapter and block from the CDC NCHS ICD-10-CM browser, FY2027)
questions.quote: Burn due to water-skis on fire, initial encounter
questions.why: It falls under water transport accidents (V90 to V94) in Chapter 20, and the final A marks the initial encounter.

questions.q: What does ICD-10-CM code V97.33XA describe?
opts: Hit by a propeller while boarding
Injured by turbulence on a commercial flight
questions.src: NLM Clinical Tables, ICD-10-CM API (chapter and block from the CDC NCHS ICD-10-CM browser, FY2027)
questions.quote: Sucked into jet engine, initial encounter
questions.why: It falls under air and space transport accidents (V95 to V97) in Chapter 20, and the final A marks the initial encounter.

questions.q: What does ICD-10-CM code W22.02XA describe?
opts: Struck by a falling street sign
questions.src: NLM Clinical Tables, ICD-10-CM API (chapter and block from the CDC NCHS ICD-10-CM browser, FY2027)
questions.quote: Walked into lamppost, initial encounter
questions.why: It falls under exposure to inanimate mechanical forces (W20 to W49) in Chapter 20, and the final A marks the initial encounter.

questions.q: What activity does ICD-10-CM code Y93.D1 record?
questions.src: NLM Clinical Tables, ICD-10-CM API (chapter and block from the CDC NCHS ICD-10-CM browser, FY2027)
questions.quote: Activity, knitting and crocheting
questions.why: Y93 codes record what the patient was doing when the injury happened, in Chapter 20, External causes of morbidity (V00 to Y99). Y93.D1 is knitting and crocheting, next to Y93.D2 for sewing. The wrong answers have codes of their own: Y93.H2 is gardening and landscaping, Y93.G3 is cooking and baking, and Y93.C2 is a handheld electronic device.

questions.q: What is a normal prothrombin time (PT) for an adult?
questions.sub: Typical lab range. Each lab sets its own.
questions.quote: Most laboratories report a normal PT reference interval of approximately 10 to 13 seconds
questions.why: Each laboratory should set or check its own interval, so a report can read a little differently; the aPTT, a separate clotting test, runs about 25 to 35 seconds.

questions.q: What is a normal activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) for an adult?
questions.sub: Typical lab range. Labs vary.
questions.quote: Normal PTT values vary between laboratories, but 25 to 35 seconds is considered normal.
questions.why: The PT, a separate clotting test, runs shorter, about 10 to 13 seconds.

questions.q: What is the normal serum albumin for an adult?
questions.sub: Typical adult range. Labs vary a little.
questions.src: Clinical Methods, 3rd edition (NCBI Bookshelf), Serum Albumin and Globulin
questions.quote: The normal serum protein level is 6 to 8 g/dl. Albumin makes up 3.5 to 5.0 g/dl, and the remainder is the total globulins.
questions.why: Albumin is the larger share of the total serum protein, which runs 6 to 8 g/dL; the globulins make up the rest.

questions.q: What is the normal total serum calcium for an adult?
questions.sub: Total calcium. Labs vary a little.
questions.quote: Most laboratories report total serum calcium concentration, with a normal range of 8.5 to 10.5 mg/dL (2.12-2.62 mmol/L).
questions.why: That is total calcium; the ionized calcium, the free share, runs 4.65 to 5.25 mg/dL on the same page.

questions.q: What is the normal serum magnesium for an adult?
questions.sub: Typical adult range. Labs vary.
questions.quote: Although reference intervals vary among laboratories, normal serum magnesium levels typically range from 1.7 to 2.2 mg/dL
questions.why: Reference intervals vary among labs: other StatPearls pages give 1.8 to 2.2 and 1.46 to 2.68 mg/dL.

questions.q: What is the normal serum phosphate for an adult?
questions.sub: Typical adult range. Labs vary a little.
questions.quote: in an adult is 2.5 to 4.5 mg/dl, and men have a slightly higher concentration than women.
questions.why: An adult level under 2.5 mg/dL is hypophosphatemia, and children run higher than adults.

questions.q: What is the normal serum creatinine for adult women?
questions.sub: Typical adult range. Labs vary a little.
questions.quote: Serum creatinine level for men with normal kidney function is approximately 0.6 to 1.2 mg/dL and between 0.5 and 1.1 mg/dL for women.
questions.why: Men run a little higher, about 0.6 to 1.2 mg/dL, because creatinine comes from muscle.

questions.q: What is the normal serum creatinine for adult men?
questions.sub: Typical adult range. Labs vary a little.
questions.quote: Serum creatinine level for men with normal kidney function is approximately 0.6 to 1.2 mg/dL and between 0.5 and 1.1 mg/dL for women.
questions.why: Women run a little lower, about 0.5 to 1.1 mg/dL, because creatinine comes from muscle.

questions.q: What is the normal hemoglobin range for adult men?
questions.sub: Typical adult range. It shifts with altitude.
questions.quote: Hemoglobin (varies with altitude) Adult men: 14 to 17 gm/dL
questions.why: The NHLBI range for adult women is 12 to 15 g/dL, and age, altitude and race can all shift normal ranges.

questions.q: What is the normal hematocrit for adult women?
questions.sub: Typical adult range. It shifts with altitude.
questions.quote: Hematocrit (varies with altitude) Adult men: 41% to 50% Adult women: 36% to 44%
questions.why: Hematocrit is the share of the blood's volume that is red cells; for adult men the NHLBI range is 41% to 50%.

questions.q: What is the normal hematocrit for adult men?
questions.sub: Typical adult range. It shifts with altitude.
questions.quote: Hematocrit (varies with altitude) Adult men: 41% to 50% Adult women: 36% to 44%
questions.why: Hematocrit is the share of the blood's volume that is red cells; for adult women the NHLBI range is 36% to 44%.

questions.q: What is a normal total serum bilirubin for an adult?
questions.sub: Typical adult level.
questions.quote: The normal serum levels of bilirubin are less than 1 milligram per deciliter (mg/dL).
questions.why: In normal blood most of it is the unconjugated form, the kind the liver has not yet processed.

questions.q: Above what blood lactate level is it called hyperlactatemia?
questions.sub: In an adult.
questions.quote: In contrast, hyperlactatemia refers to lactate levels above 2 mmol/L without associated acidosis.
questions.why: Hyperlactatemia is a high lactate without acidosis; with acidosis on top it is lactic acidosis.

questions.q: What total cholesterol does MedlinePlus call healthy for adults?
questions.sub: Adults age 20 or older.
questions.quote: Men age 20 or older: Type of Cholesterol Healthy Level Total Cholesterol Less than 200 mg/dL
questions.why: The same table sets the healthy LDL at less than 100 mg/dL, and the healthy non-HDL at less than 130 mg/dL.

questions.q: What LDL cholesterol does MedlinePlus call healthy for adults?
questions.sub: Adults age 20 or older.
questions.quote: LDL Less than 100 mg/dL
questions.why: LDL is the cholesterol that builds up in artery walls, and less than 100 mg/dL is the healthy level for adults of either sex.

questions.q: What HDL cholesterol does MedlinePlus call best for adults?
questions.sub: Adults age 20 or older.
questions.quote: Greater than or equal to 60 mg/dL is best. Levels less than 40 mg/dL are considered low.
questions.why: HDL counts as low below 40 mg/dL for men and below 50 mg/dL for women.

questions.q: What triglyceride level does MedlinePlus call healthy for adults?
questions.sub: Adults.
questions.quote: Healthy less than 150mg/dL
questions.why: On the same scale 150 to 199 mg/dL is borderline high, 200 to 499 high, and 500 or more very high.

questions.q: What A1C percentage is normal, by the cutoffs used to diagnose diabetes?
questions.sub: An adult's A1C.
questions.quote: To diagnose diabetes or prediabetes, the percentages commonly used are: Normal: A1C below 5.7%
questions.why: An A1C of 5.7% to 6.4% means prediabetes, and 6.5% or higher means diabetes.
